Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases
or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the

# Introduction {#Outlierfilter-Introduction}

Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases
or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the
price index calculation.

National Statistical Offices (NSOs) should investigate the reasons for
extreme price movement in a given dataset. If the scanner data are
thought to provide accurate price information at the product level,
outlier filters may not be required since the scanner data is considered
an accurate census of transactions. If the data are thought to include
noise in price information (from returns or reporting error), or if
there is variation in the quality or quantity of the underlying product
associated with a price, outlier removal may help exclude pricing errors
and help smooth price change due to product variations. Outlier
filtering should be more aggressive in unweighted indexes and for offer
price data (web scraped) since outlier prices in such cases are not
likely to be included in index calculations in a representative manner. 

When products are identified as outliers, it may be necessary to impute
these price movements (see section on [Treatment of missing
prices](treatment-of-missing-prices.qmd)).

There are a number of different methods available for identifying
outliers in the data. The simplest approach is to define \"fences\"
where any data that lie outside these thresholds are removed. Other
approaches are also available, although to the best of our knowledge
none of these methods are currently used in production. These methods
can be applied to price levels, or some measurement of price change (for
example, month on month; base period to current period) within a product
group in a particular time period. Because there are so many possible
combinations it is important to test fully the impact of these methods
on the final index values as it is likely to differ between different
data sources and/or product groups.

The parameters for these methods to identify outliers should be set very
carefully such that the number of outliers remains low and the setting
of the thresholds does not lead to any bias of the index results.

# User defined fences {#Outlierfilter-Userdefinedfences}

This approach creates a range of accepted values by setting a cut off
threshold (or \"fence\"). National Statistical Offices (NSOs) have
previously set these ratios to be between ratio 3 and ratio 4 (see the
section on [current
practice](current-practice-of-data-filtering.qmd)). Ratio 3
means that articles whose prices increase by more than 200% or decrease
by more than 66% are removed. In order to make sure that decimal errors
are detected the ratios should not exceed the value of 10. Of course,
the upper and the lower threshold can also not be based on a certain
ratio but instead can be chosen separately. For example, Poland has set
the upper limit for the outlier filter at factor 3 (200% price increase)
and the lower limit at 0.25 (75% price decrease). Moreover, the ratio
can be set differently depending on the product group (for example, more
volatile product groups may require a higher ratio than more stable
categories).\

Further research is needed to investigate how to detect the optimal
values for this approach. An example of research in this area is from
the Office for National Statistics (2022): [Outlier detection for rail
fares and second-hand cars dynamic price
data](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/methodologies/outlierdetectionforrailfaresandsecondhandcarsdynamicpricedata)
where the user defined fence with value 3 has since been implemented for
used cars and railfares, and subsequent follow-up research for groceries
(yet to be implemented) (2023): [Outlier detection for grocery scanner
data in consumer price
statistics](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/methodologies/outlierdetectionforgroceryscannerdatainconsumerpricestatistics)

# Other approaches {#Outlierfilter-Otherapproaches}

As an alternative to the fixed thresholds, Białek and Beręsewicz (2021)
tested removing each month all products with the lowest and the highest
one percent of all price changes within each product group. It was shown
that this alternative had a bigger impact on the index results than
fixed thresholds of ratio 3 or ratio 4.

Another option could be the use of a flexible outlier filter. A flexible
outlier filter may take the historic price development of the product
group into consideration in order to define whether a price is an
outlier or not.

Other potential methods that create a range of acceptable values are the
Tukey, kimber and k sigma approaches. These are defined as follows:

- Tukey: Tukey's rule says that the outliers are values that are more
  than 1.5 times the interquartile range from the quartiles --- i.e.,
  either below Q1 − 1.5 IQR, or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR. If Q1 and Q3 are the
  lower and upper quartiles respectively, then one could define an
  outlier to be any observation outside the range (in the standard
  implementation, k here is defined at 1.5 but it is a editable
  parameter): \[Q1 -- k(Q3-Q1), Q3 + k(Q3-Q1)\]

- Kimber: To incorporate the skewness of the distribution and possibly
  improve outlier detection, Kimber proposed fences using a constant
  multiple of the lower and the upper semi-interquartile ranges measured
  from the first and third quartile, respectively. The formula for this
  is: \[LF =Q1 -- k(𝑆𝐼𝑄𝑅𝐿), UF= Q3 + k(𝑆𝐼𝑄𝑅𝑈)\]

- K-Sigma: Given a normal distribution, k-Sigma (usually 3-sigma)
  follows the idea that nearly all values lie within 3 standard
  deviations from the mean. Any data that falls outside of this boundary
  may be determined as an outlier

Finally, there are also other more complex methods to identify outliers
that use machine learning. For example, the DBSCAN algorithm is a method
that identifies high density areas "clusters" of products. Any products
that aren't identified as a belonging to a cluster are then identified
as being outliers. For a wider review of possible methods that can be
used for outlier detection, please see previous ONS (2021)
research[.](https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/ADS_anomalydetection_technicalpanel-for-publishing.pptx)
